newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin attack on Russia monopolies seen blunt.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin attack on Russia monopolies seen blunt.

text.p: Tough words from Russian President Boris Yeltsin for the electricity, gas and rail monopolies looked more like crowd-pleasers than concrete steps towards lower prices, utility analysts said on Thursday.
In a state-of-the-nation speech to parliament, Yeltsin slammed the monopolies for charging too much money.

Officials from the world's largest gas producer Gazprom and Russia's huge grid operator United Energy System (UES) responded by saying that deep price cuts to domestic customers could lead to supply reductions.
Yeltsin singled out natural gas, electricity and rail transport as the most strategic monopolies, criticising them for raising prices too high, thus creating debts.
"This year we will take their activities under strict control of the state," he added.
Gazprom spokesman Anatoly Kotov later said that any sharp fall in gas prices would lead to output cuts, resulting in lower tax payments to the cash-strapped state.

UES spokesman Alexander Tarankov said that a cut in electricity prices without a corresponding drop in prices for heavy fuel oil to fire power stations could make power cuts in Russia's Far East a nationwide phenomenon.

But analysts doubted that Yeltsin's tough talking would mean much at all in terms of concrete steps towards lowering prices, pointing out that the Russian government had already taken measures to increase its control over monopolies.
Several referred to the creation of the Federal Energy Commission, a state regulatory body which is trying to inject market principles into energy monopolies.

"This suggests that Yeltsin's remarks were really more of a crowd-pleaser than anything else," said Jonathan Stern, vice-president of Gas Strategies in London. "Nothing concrete is likely to result from this."

The government has also announced restructuring plans both for Gazprom and UES, aimed at increasing competition in the domestic energy market and clearing the way to additional payments from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The IMF is likely to make industry restructuring a condition of additional 1997 payments. It said last month it was not yet ready to release a new tranche of its $10-billion three-year loan to Russia.

"Yeltsin's remarks were really a continuation of existing government policies, which are also an important part of the requirements of the IMF," said Anton Kudryashov, head of equity trading at Renaissance Capital.
Stern said that the main issue for Gazprom now was not prices but non-payments.
Ironically, one of its biggest debtors is UES through its majority stake in most of Russia's "energo" regional power companies, which together owe Gazprom around 20 trillion roubles ($3.5 billion).
Gazprom said last month it was seeking a one-quarter stake in UES, Russia's biggest company in terms of sales. The stake would help solve the debt problem, analysts said.
But a senior UES official said that the Anti-Monopoly Committee was unlikely to approve such an acquisition.
Analysts said price cuts should be applied to industrial users rather than domestic buyers, in line with stated government policy.
"Residential customers are paying far too little for gas," Stern said.
